title: How to Write Success Criteria: Clear Steps, Examples and Free Templates
author: Trudy Mayo
summary: Trudy Mayo, an explicit-teaching specialist, sets out a practical method for writing success criteria that turn a lesson's learning intention into observable, checkable steps. She defines success criteria as specific, measurable statements of what students must demonstrate by the end of a lesson, and distinguishes them from learning intentions, which only say what students are learning. The core of the piece is a six-step process: start from the learning intention, break the skill into steps, use specific measurable verbs, align with the assessment, phrase criteria in student-friendly language, and balance specificity with room for student choice. She illustrates the method with worked examples in maths, literacy and science, then shows how to use the criteria at the start, middle and end of a lesson, for feedback, and for self-assessment. The article closes by naming the common failures, criteria that are too vague, too broad, or detached from the lesson, and answers a short FAQ on how many criteria to write and whether students should co-construct them. It is a craft-level, classroom-ready guide rather than a research argument, though it carries some promotion of the author's free templates.
points: Mayo defines good success criteria as specific, observable actions, so vague verbs such as understand or know are replaced with demonstrable ones like identifying the numerator and denominator of a fraction.
The six-step build runs from learning intention to broken-down steps to assessment alignment, which keeps criteria tied to what students will actually be marked on.
Criteria earn their keep during the lesson, not just at the start: they anchor feedback, self-assessment checklists and an end-of-lesson review against the stated expectations.
Mayo recommends roughly three to five criteria per lesson and suggests modelling them first, then gradually letting students co-construct them to build ownership.
The three named pitfalls, too vague, too broad and not aligned to the lesson, give teachers a quick audit for their own criteria.
quotes: Success criteria are specific, measurable statements that define what students need to achieve by the end of a lesson or activity. They outline the steps or components required to meet the learning intention, so students understand the “how” behind their objective.
Avoid vague statements like “Know how to” or “Understand the topic”. Focus on what students need to demonstrate.
Learning intentions describe what students are learning. Success criteria describe what it looks like when they have achieved it.
Provide students with a checklist based on the success criteria. This helps them reflect on their progress and identify areas for improvement.
Enough to break down the skill clearly, without overwhelming students. Often three to five well written criteria are sufficient.

Success criteria are one of the most powerful parts of explicit teaching. They show students exactly what success looks like, help teachers give clearer feedback, and make learning intentions actionable.
Having clear success criteria before starting any lesson is essential. They help teachers set explicit goals for students and provide measurable benchmarks to evaluate learning outcomes.
